'Hire more staff' and 'Increase sales quickly' are actions, and 'Better quality' already has a direction built in; the right name would be 'Quality'.

mtp-w9-q10.question: In a CLD, the arrow 'Training → Skill level' carries a || mark. What does this mean?
options: The effect takes time to appear (delay)
The two variables are not related
mtp-w9-q10.explanation: Two lines (||) on an arrow show a delay: if training happens today, skill takes weeks or months to rise. Polarity is shown by + or −, not by ||. A loop's type is set by the count of negative links, not by delay, so 'becomes balancing' is wrong too.

mtp-w9-q11.question: In an office building's shared parking, every company lets as many employees as possible bring cars, thinking 'what difference will a few extra cars of ours make'. Now nobody finds a space. According to the archetype, what is the best leverage?
options: A parking quota for each company, with monitoring
Let all companies bring even more cars
Ignore it and it will fix itself in time
Give all the parking to the biggest company
mtp-w9-q11.explanation: This is the tragedy of the commons: a shared resource, individual gain for each user, and the cost spread over all. The leverage is shared rules, quotas and monitoring, as Ostrom showed that users can make rules together. More cars increase overuse, ignoring it does not stop the collapse, and giving everything to one company is unfair to the other users and creates conflict.

mtp-w9-q12.question: To save cost, a factory starts buying cheaper raw material. A few months later, defects and returns rise so much that total cost becomes even higher than before. No separate 'fundamental solution' was neglected in the story. Which archetype is this?
options: Shifting the burden: cheap material is a quick fix
Limits to growth: cost became a limiting factor
Fixes that fail: the fix's side-effect raises cost
Escalation: suppliers are in a price war with each other
mtp-w9-q12.explanation: The fix (cheap material) relieved the symptom (high cost) for now, but after a delay its unintended consequence (defects, returns) made the same problem worse: fixes that fail. Shifting the burden is the most tempting trap, but it has a separate fundamental solution that weakens because of the quick fix; the question clearly says there is none. There is no growth here and no fight between two competitors.

mtp-w9-q13.question: Loop: customers → (+) server load → (−) app speed → (+) customer satisfaction → (+) customers. What kind of loop is this, and what is its role in the limits to growth archetype?
options: Balancing (1 negative link); the limiting loop that stops growth
Reinforcing (1 negative link); the growth engine
Balancing (2 negative links); the fixes that fail loop
Reinforcing (0 negative links); success to the successful
mtp-w9-q13.explanation: Count the negative links: only server load → app speed, that is 1, which is odd, so balancing. Trace: customers up → load up → speed down → satisfaction down → customers down: this resists growth. In limits to growth this is the limiting balancing loop, while the word of mouth reinforcing loop is the growth engine. Server capacity is the limiting factor of this loop.

mtp-w9-q14.question: A school's board exam pass target is 90%, but the result comes in at 75%. Three options: (P) make next year's target 75%, (Q) start remedial classes and teacher training, (R) make internal test checking lenient so the numbers look good. According to systems thinking, what is the right analysis?
options: P and Q are symptomatic; R is the leverage
Q and R are symptomatic; P is the leverage
P is symptomatic; Q and R are both leverage
P and R lower the standard; Q is the leverage
mtp-w9-q14.explanation: P is plain eroding goals: the goal is lowered to close the gap. R also lowers the standard: the numbers look better without performance improving, which is a symptomatic fix. Q works on actual performance and holds the goal, so it is the leverage. The options that call P or R leverage turn lowering the standard into the solution itself.

mtp-w9-q15.question: A manager personally solves every urgent problem of his team. The team never learns to solve them itself, nothing happens without the manager, and now he has no time left for strategy. Which archetype is this, and what is its side-effect?
options: Fixes that fail; the fix pushed costs back up
Shifting the burden; the team's dependence on the manager
Tragedy of the commons; the manager is a shared resource
Escalation; the manager and team are fighting each other
mtp-w9-q15.explanation: The manager solving things himself is the symptomatic quick fix; the fundamental solution is building the team's capability (training, delegation), which works with a delay and has been neglected. Side-effect: the team's dependence on the manager grew, the classic sign of this archetype. Tragedy of the commons is a trap because everyone uses the manager's time, but the story is about dependence on a quick fix, not collapse from overuse.

mtp-w10-q1.question: A strategy team deliberately builds two opposing plans from the same market data ('aggressive expansion' vs 'consolidation'), holds a structured debate between them, and uses the insights from the debate to build a new combined plan. According to Churchman, which inquiring system is this?
mtp-w10-q1.explanation: Building a thesis and an antithesis from the same data, setting them against each other and drawing out a synthesis is Hegelian (dialectical) inquiry. Kantian is the trap: it also uses several models, but they are complementary and compared for best fit, not deliberately opposed.

mtp-w10-q2.question: Which of these situations is best suited to a hard systems approach?
options: Minimising delivery cost with fixed routes and known demand
Settling a dispute among stakeholders over a city's development priorities
Disagreement over what a hospital's purpose should be
mtp-w10-q2.explanation: A hard systems approach works when the goal is clear and agreed and the problem is well defined; minimising delivery cost is a classic optimisation problem. In the other three, the stakeholders' goals and worldviews themselves differ, which is the territory of the soft systems approach.

mtp-w10-q3.question: In Checkland's soft systems methodology, what is the 'W' in CATWOE?
options: Workers who carry out the transformation
Weltanschauung: the worldview that makes the transformation meaningful
Wastage that occurs in the process
mtp-w10-q3.explanation: W = Weltanschauung (a German word meaning worldview): the perspective in which this transformation makes sense. Different worldviews give different root definitions, and SSM compares them. Workers is the trap, because the people who carry out the transformation fall under 'A' (actors).

mtp-w10-q4.question: A marketing team surveys 2,000 customers and treats whatever the data and the whole team agree on as 'what customers really prefer'. Which inquiring system is this?
mtp-w10-q4.explanation: Starting from observations (survey data) and treating the community's consensus as 'truth' is Lockean inquiry. Leibnizian is the trap because both seem 'systematic', but Leibnizian reasoning draws conclusions from assumptions and logic, not from data.

mtp-w10-q5.question: A factory canteen gets very crowded at 1 pm. Of Ackoff's four ways, which option 'dissolves' the problem?
options: Do nothing and hope the crowd reduces by itself
Open one extra counter, as was done last time
Use a queueing model to work out the optimal number of counters
Stagger the lunch timings of departments so that the crowd never forms
mtp-w10-q5.explanation: To dissolve means to redesign the system so the problem never arises; staggered lunch timings remove the 1 pm peak altogether. Doing nothing is absolving, an extra counter from experience is resolving, and finding the optimum with a queueing model is solving. Trap: solving, because it seems the most 'scientific', but it accepts the crowd and only deals with it.

mtp-w10-q6.question: A forecasting team builds three different models for next year's demand (time-series trend, regression on GDP, and an expert panel), tests all three on the same past data, and chooses the model that explains the data best. Which inquiring system is this?
mtp-w10-q6.explanation: Building several alternative models of the same problem and choosing the best fit is Kantian inquiry, which brings theory and data together. Hegelian is the most tempting trap, but there the views are deliberately opposed and a synthesis comes from debate; here the models compete rather than clash. Lockean would rely only on data and consensus, not on alternative theories.

mtp-w10-q7.question: An analyst starts from some fixed assumptions (constant demand, constant price, a given cost formula) and uses maths to find the 'optimal' production quantity, without looking at any new data. According to Churchman, which inquiring system is this?
mtp-w10-q7.explanation: Drawing conclusions from assumptions (axioms) through logic and formulas is Leibnizian inquiry; 'truth' is whatever is consistent within the model. Lockean works from data and consensus, which is not happening here. Remember the weakness: if the assumptions are wrong, the model's 'optimum' will be wrong too.

mtp-w10-q8.question: A manager ignores the office printer's repeated jams and assumes the problem will fix itself. According to Ackoff, which way of treating a problem is this?
mtp-w10-q8.explanation: Ignoring a problem and hoping it goes away by itself is absolving. Resolving is a 'good enough' answer from experience, solving is an optimal answer from research, and dissolving is redesigning the system so the problem disappears. Trap: dissolve, because both talk of the problem 'vanishing'; but dissolving involves a redesign, absolving involves nothing.

mtp-w10-q9.question: In Checkland's soft systems methodology, what is the 'A' in CATWOE?
options: Actors: those who carry out the transformation
Authority: whoever takes the final decision
mtp-w10-q9.explanation: A = actors, the people who actually carry out the transformation (such as the canteen workers). The power to make the final decision or stop the system lies with the owners (O), so the 'authority' option confuses A with O. Assumptions and analysis are not CATWOE letters at all.

mtp-w10-q10.question: A city planning team keeps refining its air pollution model every year with new data, health experts' views and ethical questions ('safe for whom?'), and believes the inquiry will never be 'final'. Which inquiring system is this?
mtp-w10-q10.explanation: Open-ended inquiry that keeps refining itself, sweeps in other disciplines and ethics, and asks 'for whom' is Singerian. Kantian is a trap, because it also has models and data; but Kantian compares several models, picks the best fit and stops, while here the inquiry never ends.

mtp-w10-q11.question: A warehouse manager, from 15 years of experience, says: 'Hire 10 temporary workers in peak season; it always works.' He does no model or data analysis. According to Ackoff, which approach is this?
mtp-w10-q11.explanation: Giving a 'good enough' answer from experience and common sense is resolving. Solving would be finding the optimal number with data and models. Absolving is doing nothing, and dissolving is redesigning the system so the peak problem never arises (such as spreading orders across the year).

mtp-w10-q12.question: A company's 5 senior managers fully agree on a market survey report, treat it as 'what customers really want', and make a big launch. The launch fails, and it turns out the survey was done only in metro cities. Which inquiring system's weakness shows here?
options: Lockean: everyone can agree even on wrong data
Leibnizian: the model's starting axioms were wrong
Hegelian: there was no debate of opposing plans
mtp-w10-q12.explanation: Step 1: the team took the data (survey) and its own consensus as 'truth', which is Lockean inquiry. Step 2: Lockean's weakness is that a community can agree even on wrong or biased data, and it assumes the data is clean by itself; here the sample was metro-only. Leibnizian is the assumptions-to-logic system, which was not used here. A Hegelian debate might have helped, but the question is about the weakness of the system actually used.

mtp-w10-q13.question: SSM root definition: 'A municipality-owned system that collects and recycles city residents' waste through the contractor's teams, in the belief that a clean city is every citizen's right, within the budget and pollution laws.' Which CATWOE elements are 'the contractor's teams' and 'a clean city is every citizen's right', in order?
mtp-w10-q13.explanation: The contractor's teams actually carry out the transformation (collecting and recycling waste), so they are actors (A). 'A clean city is every citizen's right' is the worldview that makes the transformation meaningful: Weltanschauung (W). The customers are the residents and the owner is the municipality. Trap: taking the belief as the transformation; T is turning an input into an output (a city with waste → clean, recycled), not a belief.

mtp-w10-q14.question: A company faces three tasks: (1) computing a loan EMI with a given formula, (2) building several forecasting models for a new product's demand, comparing them and picking the best fit, (3) holding a debate between two opposing teams on 'should we acquire the competitor or not' and drawing a synthesis. Which inquiring systems suit them best, in order?
mtp-w10-q14.explanation: (1) Deduction from a fixed formula: Leibnizian, which is perfect for a well-structured problem. (2) Several alternative models and the best fit to data: Kantian. (3) Synthesis from thesis vs antithesis: Hegelian. The second option calls (2) Lockean, but Lockean is consensus on one data set, not a comparison of different models. Lesson: inquiring systems are not replacements for each other but tools for different problems.

mtp-w10-q15.question: At a university there is a shortage of library seats during exams, and students, faculty and the administration see the problem completely differently. A consultant first draws a rich picture and writes root definitions for each group's worldview. In the end he suggests staggering departments' exams so that not everyone's exams fall together and the seat crunch never arises. What are the approach and Ackoff's method, in order?
mtp-w10-q15.explanation: Step 1: the stakeholders' worldviews differ and the consultant uses a rich picture and root definitions: this is the soft systems approach (SSM). Step 2: redesigning the exam schedule so the peak demand disappears is dissolving. Resolving would be adding a few temporary seats from experience, and solving would be finding the optimal number of seats with a model. Hard systems assumes an agreed goal, which is missing here.

mtp-w11-q1.question: 'UdaanSasta Air' (fictional) uses only one aircraft type, gives no free meals, sells tickets only online and keeps aircraft turnaround times short, so that its fares are the lowest in the industry. According to Porter, which strategy is this?
mtp-w11-q1.explanation: Designing every activity for the lowest cost and offering the cheapest option to a broad market is cost leadership. In differentiation the customer pays more for a unique feature, which is not the case here. Focus would apply if the airline targeted only a narrow segment.

mtp-w11-q2.question: A startup's open-plan office, bean bags, casual dress code and Friday team lunches belong to which level of culture in Schein's model?
mtp-w11-q2.explanation: Things you can see (layout, dress code, rituals) are artifacts, the topmost level of culture. To understand what they mean you have to look at the deeper levels. Espoused values is the trap: those are written or stated values (such as 'we value openness'), not physical things.

mtp-w11-q3.question: A company falls under Section 135. Its net profit in the last three financial years was ₹40 crore, ₹50 crore and ₹90 crore. What is the minimum CSR spend required this year?
mtp-w11-q3.explanation: Average net profit = (40 + 50 + 90) ÷ 3 = 180 ÷ 3 = ₹60 crore. CSR = 2% × 60 = ₹1.2 crore. ₹1.8 crore is 2% of the latest year (90), ₹3.6 crore is 2% of the three-year total (180), and ₹1 crore is 2% of the middle year (50).

mtp-w11-q4.question: 'Triveni Group' (fictional) used to make only soap and ran on a functional structure (one production head, one marketing head). It has now diversified into FMCG, hotels and IT services, and decisions have become very slow. What would Chandler suggest?
options: Keep the functional structure, because structure should never change
Adopt a divisional structure, because structure should change to fit the new strategy
Change the strategy to fit the old structure
Centralise all decisions with the CEO
mtp-w11-q4.explanation: Chandler's finding was that structure follows strategy: after diversification, a separate division for each business (with its own production and marketing) is more effective. The third option reverses the relationship, and centralisation would make slow decisions even slower.

mtp-w11-q5.question: A bank announces a new strategy: 'customer-centric innovation'. But approvals still need 7 signatures, managers' bonuses are tied only to cost-cutting, and top leadership's style is command-and-control. Using McKinsey's 7S, what is the diagnosis?
options: Only strategy matters, so everything is fine
There is a misfit: systems, style and shared values do not support the new strategy
The problem is only the number of staff
mtp-w11-q5.explanation: 7S says the seven elements must fit one another. The approval process and bonuses are systems, the command style is 'style', and all three work against innovation. Only the strategy has changed, on paper, so results will not follow. Staff numbers are not even mentioned here.

mtp-w11-q6.question: A pharma company follows all pollution and drug laws. Beyond that, it publicly shares all side-effect data for its medicine, even though the law does not require this much, because it is fair to patients. In Carroll's pyramid, which level is this extra step?
mtp-w11-q6.explanation: Going beyond the law to run its core business fairly and rightly is ethical responsibility. Following laws is the legal level, which the company already does. Philanthropic is the most tempting trap, but it concerns voluntary giving and community programmes (such as a donation to a hospital), not honest information about one's own product.

mtp-w11-q7.question: A premium headphones brand charges 40% more than competitors because of its unique sound quality and design, and customers happily pay it. Which of Porter's generic strategies is this?
mtp-w11-q7.explanation: Offering something unique that customers pay more for is differentiation. In cost leadership the company competes on the lowest cost and price, which is the opposite here. Stuck in the middle would be a company that is neither the cheapest nor unique, while here the choice is clear.

mtp-w11-q8.question: Before rolling out new software, the CEO shows data at a town hall on how many orders the old system loses every month, so that everyone understands the need for change. Which stage of Lewin's model is this?
mtp-w11-q8.explanation: Explaining the need for change and loosening old habits is the unfreeze stage. In the change stage new ways are actually introduced (training, rollout), and in refreeze the new behaviour is locked in through systems and rewards. Feedback is not one of Lewin's three stages.

mtp-w11-q9.question: A company uses its profit to build a library in a village. No law requires it and it is not linked to the company's business. Which level of Carroll's CSR pyramid is this?
mtp-w11-q9.explanation: A voluntary contribution to the community, not required by law and not linked to the core business, is philanthropic responsibility. The ethical level is about running one's own business fairly. Trap: ethical, because building a library is a 'good deed'; but it is a donation, not fair conduct of the business.

mtp-w11-q10.question: In the last financial year a company had a net worth of ₹300 crore, a turnover of ₹800 crore and a net profit of ₹6 crore. Do the Section 135 CSR rules apply to it?
options: No, because its net worth is below ₹500 crore
Yes, because its net profit is above the ₹5 crore limit
No, because all three conditions must be met together
No, because its turnover is below ₹1,000 crore
mtp-w11-q10.explanation: Section 135 applies when any one of three conditions is met: net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more. The net profit is ₹6 crore, above ₹5 crore, so the rules apply. The biggest trap is 'all three conditions together'; it is an 'or' rule, not an 'and' rule. The net worth and turnover options stop after seeing one condition fail.

mtp-w11-q11.question: A company's website says 'We value work-life balance'. But everyone knows that whoever is not seen online until 11 at night does not get promoted, and nobody says this openly. In Schein's model, at which level is the belief 'staying online late at night is real commitment'?
options: Artifacts, which are visible from outside
Espoused values, what the company says
mtp-w11-q11.explanation: A deep, unspoken belief that drives actual behaviour (promotions) is a basic underlying assumption. The website's 'We value work-life balance' is an espoused value, what the company says. Trap: espoused values, because the question talks about values; but the real culture sits at the lower level, and it contradicts the stated value.

mtp-w11-q12.question: A company falls under Section 135. In the last three financial years its net profit was ₹80 crore, a loss of ₹20 crore, and ₹100 crore. What is the minimum CSR spend required this year (rounded to 2 decimal places)?
mtp-w11-q12.explanation: In the average net profit, a loss counts as negative: (80 − 20 + 100) ÷ 3 = 160 ÷ 3 ≈ ₹53.33 crore. CSR = 2% × 53.33 ≈ ₹1.07 crore. ₹1.2 crore comes from treating the loss as zero, (80 + 100) ÷ 3 = 60; ₹1.8 crore from averaging only the two profitable years (90); and ₹2 crore is just 2% of the latest year (100).

mtp-w11-q13.question: 'Dhaaga Fabrics' (fictional) has so far made cheap cloth for the mass market through cost leadership. Now it also wants to sell premium designer fabrics, but with the same factory, the same sales team and the same cost-cutting bonus system. What is the biggest risk?
options: No risk; both strategies run together easily
Only the risk of a focus strategy, since the premium market is narrow
Stuck in the middle, plus a 7S misfit: old bonus systems and skills
Only the risk of missing Lewin's refreeze stage
mtp-w11-q13.explanation: For Porter, a company that chases both cost and differentiation without a clear choice can get stuck in the middle. Add the 7S lens: the new strategy (premium) comes with old systems (cost-cutting bonus), skills (mass production team) and style, so the strategy will stay on paper. The focus option sees only one part and ignores the misfit; refreeze is the stage after a change, which has not even started.

mtp-w11-q14.question: A manager must decide the price of an essential medicine. Three arguments come up: (1) 'Set the price that gives the greatest benefit to the greatest number', (2) 'Every patient has a basic right to essential medicine', (3) 'Charge all patients with the same illness the same, fair price'. Which ethical approaches are these, in order?
mtp-w11-q14.explanation: (1) The greatest benefit for the greatest number: utilitarian. (2) Respecting every person's basic right: rights. (3) Fair and equal treatment: justice. The third option swaps (2) and (3), the most common trap because 'right' and 'fair' both sound like justice; the difference is that rights is about each individual's entitlement, justice about the fairness of distribution.

mtp-w11-q15.question: A company launched a new 'customer-first' process, trained everyone, and at first people started working the new way. After 6 months everyone went back to the old way, because appraisal and bonus were still based only on call speed. Which of Lewin's stages was weak, and what is the fix?
options: Unfreeze; hold more town halls to explain the need
Refreeze; link appraisal and rewards to the new behaviour
No stage; people always resist change
mtp-w11-q15.explanation: Unfreeze and change both happened: people had adopted the new way. The problem was that the new behaviour was not locked in through systems and rewards, which is refreeze's job; the old incentives pulled people back. This is also the 7S point: systems must fit the strategy. More training is a trap: there was no lack of skill, only an incentive mismatch.

mtp-w12-q1.question: Which of these thinker and idea pairs is correct?
options: Fayol: scientific management and time study
mtp-w12-q1.explanation: The differential piece-rate is part of Taylor's scientific management. The Hawthorne studies are linked to Mayo, the 14 principles are Fayol's, and scientific management is Taylor's. The other three options swap names and ideas, a common exam trap.

mtp-w12-q2.question: Which of these is a business (functional) area rather than a management function?
mtp-w12-q2.explanation: Marketing is a functional area (department). Planning, organising and controlling are management functions carried out inside every department: marketing, finance, HR and so on. Trap: the word 'function' appears in both, so check whether the question is about an activity or an area.

mtp-w12-q3.question: A factory supervisor pays a bonus for meeting the daily target, but finds that the workers' group keeps its own output limit and taunts anyone who goes beyond it. Which research first highlighted informal group norms like this?
options: The bank wiring room observation in the Hawthorne studies
mtp-w12-q3.explanation: In the bank wiring room of the Hawthorne studies, researchers saw that the group had set its own output norm and people did not exceed it despite incentives. Taylor is the trap, because Taylor also talked about workers deliberately working slowly (soldiering), but his answer was time study and piece rates, not an analysis of the social group.

mtp-w12-q4.question: In a city, whenever accidents rise, extra traffic police are deployed. Accidents fall for a while, then rise again, and the budget for improving road design is cut every year because 'the police are managing'. Which archetype is this?
mtp-w12-q4.explanation: Extra police is the symptomatic quick fix and road redesign the fundamental solution. As reliance on the quick fix grew, the fundamental solution's budget kept being cut: this is shifting the burden. Tragedy of the commons is tempting because roads are shared, but the story here is dependence on a quick fix, not overuse of a resource.

mtp-w12-q5.question: In a board meeting the CFO says: 'We have already spent ₹50 crore on this plant, so we have to finish it.' A director asks: 'If we were starting from zero today, would we put the next ₹30 crore here?' Which bias is the director guarding against?
mtp-w12-q5.explanation: The director's question sets aside the ₹50 crore (which cannot be recovered) and moves the decision to the future ₹30 crore and its benefits, which is the direct cure for the sunk cost fallacy. Anchoring is the trap because ₹50 crore is a big number, but the CFO's argument is not about a number pulling an estimate; it is about using past spending as a reason.

mtp-w12-q6.question: A state government wants to reduce stubble burning. Farmers, agricultural scientists, officials and city residents see the issue in completely different ways, and there is no agreement on a single objective. According to the course, what is the most suitable approach?
options: Hard systems optimisation with a single cost function from the start
A Taylor-style time study of farmers' work
Only Weber-style strict rules and penalties
A soft systems approach: understand the situation with a rich picture and root definitions (CATWOE) for different worldviews, then agree on feasible and desirable changes
mtp-w12-q6.explanation: When stakeholders' goals and worldviews differ and the problem itself is disputed, it is a messy, soft situation; SSM first brings out the different perspectives and then looks for agreed changes. Hard optimisation is the most tempting trap, but it first needs an agreed objective, which is missing here. Imposing rules alone also ignores the worldviews that are the reason rules are not followed.

mtp-w12-q7.question: 'The manager had little time and information, so he chose the first reasonably good option.' Whose idea is this?
mtp-w12-q7.explanation: Choosing the first 'good enough' option under limited time and information is Herbert Simon's satisficing, which comes from bounded rationality. Taylor spoke of finding the 'one best way', the opposite of satisficing. Fayol and Weber are thinkers of structure and principles, not of the limits of decision making.

mtp-w12-q8.question: A company combines a phone cover and a wallet into a 'wallet case'. Which tool and letter is this?
mtp-w12-q8.explanation: Joining two existing things into a new product is SCAMPER's Combine. SWOT looks at a company's internal and external position, Pareto prioritises causes, and five whys finds a root cause; none of these is a tool for designing a new product.

mtp-w12-q9.question: A consultant answers every question with: 'It depends: on the company's size, technology and environment.' Which approach is this?
mtp-w12-q9.explanation: 'It depends' and designing to fit the situation are the core of the contingency approach. Scientific management and bureaucracy both thought of one 'best' model applied everywhere. The quantitative approach improves decisions with mathematical models, but 'it depends on the situation' is not its central idea.

mtp-w12-q10.question: The head of the marketing department compares actual sales with the target every month and takes corrective action when there is a deviation. Which management function is this, and in which business area is it happening?
mtp-w12-q10.explanation: Comparing actuals with a standard and taking corrective action is controlling, and it is happening in the marketing department. That is the course's point: management functions run inside every business area. Trap: linking controlling to finance, because numbers and targets look like finance; but the work is the marketing head's.

mtp-w12-q11.question: A board's chairman gives his opinion first in every meeting, and after that no director speaks against him, even when they have doubts. What is the problem and what is the most direct remedy?
options: Anchoring; the chairman should never mention a number
Sunk cost; remove past spending from the discussion
Confirmation bias; look only at data that agrees
Groupthink; chairman speaks last, add a devil's advocate
mtp-w12-q11.explanation: Staying silent despite doubts and appearing 'all agreed' behind the leader is groupthink. Janis's remedies: the leader gives his view last, and someone is made devil's advocate. Anchoring is a trap because the chairman's first opinion pulls judgement; but anchoring is about a starting number, and the real issue here is dissent being suppressed in the group.

mtp-w12-q12.question: Case: (1) a strategy team pitted opposing 'go premium' and 'go cheap' plans built from the same data against each other and drew a new combined plan from the debate; (2) when the company diversified into many new businesses, it set up a separate division for each; (3) when the sales target was missed again and again, the target itself was lowered. Which concepts are these, in order?
options: Hegelian inquiry; Chandler's structure follows strategy; eroding goals
Kantian inquiry; contingency approach; shifting the burden
Hegelian inquiry; Fayol's unity of direction; fixes that fail
Lockean inquiry; Chandler's structure follows strategy; eroding goals
mtp-w12-q12.explanation: (1) A debate of opposing views and a synthesis: Hegelian (in Kantian, complementary models are compared for best fit, not pitted against each other). (2) The strategy (diversification) changed, so the structure became divisional: Chandler. (3) Lowering the goal to close the gap: eroding goals. The third option calls (3) fixes that fail, but there the fix's side-effect brings the problem back; here the goal itself was moved. The fourth option calls (1) Lockean, which is the consensus system, not the debate one.

mtp-w12-q13.question: A company is under Section 135. In the last three financial years its net profit was ₹180 crore, ₹240 crore and ₹300 crore. This year it spent ₹4 crore on CSR. By how much did it fall short of the required minimum?
mtp-w12-q13.explanation: Average net profit = (180 + 240 + 300) ÷ 3 = 720 ÷ 3 = ₹240 crore. Required CSR = 2% × 240 = ₹4.8 crore. Shortfall = 4.8 − 4 = ₹0.8 crore. ₹2 crore comes from taking 2% of only the latest year (300) = ₹6 crore, and ₹10.4 crore from taking 2% of the three-year total (720) = ₹14.4 crore. 'No shortfall' would only look right if 2% were applied to some smaller base.

mtp-w12-q14.question: A startup's orders are growing fast, but its customer support team stays the same size; tickets start piling up, ratings fall, and then growth stalls. The founder still raises ad spend and says: 'We have already put ₹2 crore into ads, we can't stop now.' Which archetype and which bias are showing?
options: Limits to growth; sunk cost fallacy
mtp-w12-q14.explanation: Archetype: the reinforcing growth loop hit the limit of support capacity, and a balancing loop (pending tickets, ratings) stopped growth: limits to growth. The leverage is adding support capacity, not ads. Bias: 'we have already put in ₹2 crore' makes past spending the reason for a future decision: sunk cost fallacy. ₹2 crore is a number, but it is not pulling any estimate, so anchoring is a trap.

mtp-w12-q15.question: A hospital has two problems: (1) making a minimum-cost nurse shift roster with known demand, a goal everyone agrees on; (2) deep disagreement among doctors, management and the local community about what the new wing's purpose should be. Which pairing is most correct?
mtp-w12-q15.explanation: (1) The goal is clear and agreed and the problem well-defined, so the hard systems approach (optimisation, such as a scheduling model). (2) The stakeholders' worldviews and goals differ, so the soft systems approach (rich picture, CATWOE) is needed first. The first option swaps them. 'Hard for both' is the most common trap: in (2) there is no agreed objective to optimise.
